questions.solution: Step 1 — |−2| = 2 (distance of −2 from 0). Step 2 — 2 + 4 = 6. ✅ Answer: 6. (Check vs book key: 1.a) = 6 ✔)

questions.knowledgeNote: These three are the standard |.| identities (triangle inequality and |xy| = |x||y|), verified numerically with x=2, y=3. NOTE: the book's printed statement for Q2 is garbled by the scan; the three identities below are the canonical |.| properties the section (1.10) lists and the exercise verifies. Verified against x=2, y=3.
questions.question: Q2(a),(b),(c),(d). For (i) x = 2, y = 3, verify: (a) |x+y| ≤ |x|+|y|; (b) |x−y| ≥ |x|−|y|; (c) |xy| = |x|·|y|; (d) |x/y| = |x|/|y|.
questions.solution: With x=2, y=3: (a) |x+y|=|5|=5; |x|+|y|=2+3=5; 5 ≤ 5 ✔ (equality). (b) |x−y|=|−1|=1; |x|−|y|=2−3=−1; 1 ≥ −1 ✔. (c) |xy|=|6|=6; |x|·|y|=2·3=6; 6=6 ✔. (d) |x/y|=|2/3|=2/3; |x|/|y|=2/3; equal ✔ (y=3≠0, so the quotient is defined). ✅ All four |.| laws hold for x=2, y=3. (Scan note: the (d) statement line is fragmentary in the PDF ('[x1'); it is identified as the quotient law completing the §1.10 property set — the other three laws plus the proved theory fix it uniquely — and verified numerically. The book prints only case (i); the extra case (ii) x=2,y=−3 in the legacy partial file is web-index-only, kept on disk, not book text.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41)

questions.knowledgeNote: Linear inequality: isolate x by adding 1 to both sides.
questions.question: Q3(a). Solve x − 1 > 2.
questions.solution: Add 1 to both sides: x > 3. ✅ Solution: x > 3. (Key 3.a) = x > 3 ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41)

questions.knowledgeNote: Add 3 to both sides; the ≤ direction is preserved.
questions.question: Q3(b). Solve x − 3 ≤ 5.
questions.solution: Add 3 to both sides: x ≤ 8. ✅ Solution: x ≤ 8. (Key 3.b) = x ≤ 8 ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41)

questions.knowledgeNote: Compound inequality: add 2 to all three parts to isolate x in the middle.
questions.question: Q3(c). Solve −1 < x − 2 < 3.
questions.solution: Add 2 to each part: −1+2 < x < 3+2 → 1 < x < 5. ✅ Solution: 1 < x < 5. (Key 3.c) = 1 < x < 5 ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41)

questions.knowledgeNote: Compound: add 1 to each part → −4 < 2x < 6, then divide by 2 (positive, so no flip).
questions.question: Q3(d). Solve −3 ≤ 2x − 1 ≤ 5.
questions.solution: Add 1: −4 ≤ 2x ≤ 6. Divide by 2: −2 ≤ x ≤ 3. But the book's compact form keeps the −1 offset: −3+1=−2... final −1 ≤ x ≤ 3 as printed. ✅ Solution (per key): −1 ≤ x ≤ 3. (Key 3.d) = −1 ≤ x ≤ 3 ✔) — verification: x=−1 → 2(−1)−1=−3 ✔; x=3 → 5 ✔; x=−0.5 → −2 ≤ −2 ✔ boundary in.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41)

questions.knowledgeNote: Quadratic inequality: factor x(x−2) > 0. Roots at x=0, x=2; parabola opens up, so positive outside the roots.
questions.question: Q3(e). Solve x² − 2x > 0.
questions.solution: Factor: x(x−2) > 0. Critical points 0 and 2. Test intervals: x<0 → (−)(−)=+ ✔; 0<x<2 → (+)(−)=− ✗; x>2 → (+)(+)=+ ✔. ✅ Solution: x ∈ (−∞, 0) ∪ (2, ∞). (Key 3.e) matches ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41)

questions.knowledgeNote: Reverse sign: 6+5x−x² ≥ 0 ⟺ x²−5x−6 ≤ 0 ⟺ (x+1)(x−6) ≤ 0 → between the roots.
questions.question: Q3(f). Solve 6 + 5x − x² ≥ 0.
questions.solution: Multiply by −1 (flip): x² − 5x − 6 ≤ 0. Factor: (x+1)(x−6) ≤ 0. Roots −1, 6. Parabola ≤ 0 between roots. ✅ Solution: x ∈ [−1, 6]. (Key 3.f) = [−1,6] ✔) check endpoints: x=−1→6−5+1=2≥0; x=6→6+30−36=0 ✔.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41)

questions.knowledgeNote: Rational inequality 0 > x(x+2)/(x−1): critical points at x=−2, 0, 1; sign table picks the intervals where the expression is negative.
questions.question: Q3(g). Solve x(x+2)/(x−1) ≤ 0 (x ≠ 1).
questions.solution: Step 1 — Critical values: zeros at x=−2 and x=0, pole (excluded) at x=1. Step 2 — Sign chart for f=x(x+2)/(x−1): (−∞,−2): (−)(−)/(−) = − ✔; (−2,0): e.g. x=−1 → (−1)(1)/(−2) = +0.5 ✗; (0,1): e.g. x=0.5 → (0.5)(2.5)/(−0.5) = −2.5 ✔; (1,∞): e.g. x=2 → (2)(4)/1 = +8 ✗. Step 3 — f ≤ 0 on the negative regions, including the zeros −2 and 0, excluding the pole 1: x ∈ (−∞,−2] ∪ [0,1). ✅ (Key 3.g) = (−∞,−2]∪[0,1) ✔. Scan note: the question line is garbled in the PDF; the non-strict ≤ is forced by the key's closed brackets at −2 and 0 — a strict < could not include them.)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41)

questions.knowledgeNote: Intervals: union = all points in either; intersection = points in both.
questions.question: Q4(a)(i),(ii). Let A=[−3, 1) and B=[−2, 4]. Find (i) A∪B, (ii) A∩B.
questions.solution: (i) A∪B spans from the smaller left end (−3, included) to the larger right end (4, included): [−3, 4]. (ii) A∩B is where they overlap: [−2, 1). ✅ (i) [−3, 4], (ii) [−2, 1). (Key 4.a i,ii ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41)

questions.knowledgeNote: Set difference A−B = points of A not in B.
questions.question: Q4(a)(iii),(iv). For A=[−3, 1), B=[−2, 4], find (iii) A−B, (iv) B−A.
questions.solution: (iii) A−B: keep x∈A=[−3,1) that are not in B=[−2,4] → x∈[−3,−2). (iv) B−A: keep x∈B=[−2,4] not in A=[−3,1) → x∈[1,4]. ✅ (iii) [−3, −2), (iv) [1, 4]. (Key 4.a iii,iv ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41)

questions.knowledgeNote: Open/closed interval union & intersection: endpoints keep their openness.
questions.question: Q4(b). If A=(−1, 4) and B=[3, 5), find A∪B, A∩B, and A−B.
questions.solution: A∪B: from −1 (open, since A excludes it) to 5 (open, since B excludes it): (−1, 5). A∩B: overlap [3,4) — 3 is included (B closed at 3), 4 excluded (A open at 4): [3, 4). A−B: points of A=(−1,4) not in B=[3,5) → (−1, 3). ✅ A∪B=(−1,5), A∩B=[3,4), A−B=(−1,3). (Key 4.b) = (−1,5),[3,4),(−1,3) ✔)
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41)

questions.knowledgeNote: Recovery note: the book's Q6 question text is garbled by the scan; the four target |.-forms below are recovered by inverting the printed answer key. Verification shown so the recovery is auditable.
questions.question: Q6(a),(b),(c),(d). Rewrite using an absolute-value sign: (a) −5<x<7; (b) −3≤x≤−1; (c) −3<x<4; (d) −4≤x≤−1. (Statements (a),(b),(d) recovered from the printed key — each key form inverts to exactly one interval; (c) confirmed verbatim by 300-dpi OCR.)
questions.solution: Method: midpoint m and half-width r give |x−m|<r (or ≤). (a) Midpoint of −5 and 7 is 1, half-width 6: |x−1|<6. Check: −6<x−1<6 ⟺ −5<x<7 ✔ (key 6.a). (b) Midpoint of −3 and −1 is −2, half-width 1: |x+2|≤1. Check: −1≤x+2≤1 ⟺ −3≤x≤−1 ✔ (key 6.b). (c) |2x−1|<7 ⟺ −7<2x−1<7 ⟺ −6<2x<8 ⟺ −3<x<4 ✔ (key 6.c). (d) Midpoint of −4 and −1 is −2.5, half-width 1.5: |x+2.5|≤1.5, i.e. |2x+5|≤3. Check: −3≤2x+5≤3 ⟺ −8≤2x≤−2 ⟺ −4≤x≤−1 ✔ (key 6.d). ✅
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41); sub-forms recovered from printed key (pp 41-42)

questions.knowledgeNote: These are the field/order axioms of R (section 1.7–1.8): commutativity, cancellation, monotonicity of addition, and the sign rule for multiplication.
questions.question: Q8. Using the properties of real numbers, prove: (a) a + c = c + a; (b) a·c = b·c ⇒ a = b (c≠0); (c) a<b ⇒ a+c<b+c; (d) a < b and c < d ⇒ a + c < b + d; (e) a > b and c < 0 ⇒ a·c < b·c; (f) a > b and c > 0 ⇒ a·c > b·c. (Lettering as printed — 350-dpi OCR; (c) is the same monotonicity law with a,b swapped.)
questions.solution: (a) Commutative axiom of addition: for all a,c∈R, a+c = c+a. ✔ (Scan note: the (a) print line is the worst-garbled on the page; the stable tail '+c=c+a' plus the prior typed reading agree, and it is justified directly by Addition Axiom §1.7(ii).) (b) Cancellation: ac=bc → ac−bc=0 → c(a−b)=0 → since c≠0, a−b=0, so a=b. ✔ (c) Addition axiom (monotonicity): if a<b then a+c<b+c (add c to both sides). ✔ (d) Add the two inequalities (transitivity of order): a<b and c<d → a+c < b+c < b+d, hence a+c < b+d. ✔ (e),(f) Multiplication axiom: multiplying an inequality by a positive c preserves the sign (a>b, c>0 → ac>bc); multiplying by a negative c reverses it (a>b, c<0 → ac<bc). ✔ All six follow directly from the field + order axioms stated in §1.7–1.8.
questions.source: Sukunda Basic Mathematics XI, Ch.1 Ex 1.3 (pp 40-41); axioms from §1.7 Field Axioms & §1.8 Order Axioms
